question.worked_solution:
Let $u=x+3.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that $x=u-3.$ 

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $1$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $4$ | $9$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{6}\frac{3x+1}{\sqrt{x+3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{4}^{9}\frac{3(u-3)+1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{9}\frac{3u-8}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{9}(3{u}^{1/2}-8{u}^{-1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={(\frac{3}{(3/2)}{u}^{3/2}-\frac{8}{(1/2)}{u}^{1/2})|}_{4}^{9} \\  & ={(2{u}^{3/2}-16{u}^{1/2})|}_{4}^{9} \\  & =(2\cdot {9}^{3/2}-16\cdot {9}^{1/2})-(2\cdot {4}^{3/2}-16\cdot {4}^{1/2}) \\  & =(2\cdot 27-16\cdot 3)-(2\cdot 8-16\cdot 2) \\  & =(54-48)-(16-32) \\  & =6-(-16) \\  & =22\end{aligned}
$$
